transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thank you. Um, so I'm here because... well, honestly, I'm just kind of at my breaking point with myself. I just graduated college, right? And I'm supposed to be doing all these normal, everyday adult things now, but I just... I can't seem to keep track of anything. 

What finally made me actually make this appointment—and actually show up for it, which is honestly a miracle in itself—is that I keep forgetting these really basic things. Like, paying my bills on time, or, God, returning emails for job interviews. I'll see the email from a recruiter, tell myself I'm going to reply in exactly five minutes after I finish whatever I'm doing, and then literally a week goes by and I realize I've completely ghosted a hiring manager. It’s so embarrassing. And it's not just that, it's showing up for appointments, or even just following through on stupid little errands like going to the post office or picking something up from the store. I'll leave the house with a plan and then just... completely forget what I was supposed to be doing or get totally derailed. 

It’s just... it's starting to really cost me real opportunities, like, actual jobs that I desperately need right now since I'm not working, and my credit score is probably tanking because of the late bills. I just feel like I'm constantly dropping the ball and apologizing to people, and I just don't know why I can't just remember to do things and function like a normal person.
How are these memory and organization issues affecting your overall mood and well-being?

Honestly? It’s... well, it’s completely exhausting. It just makes me feel awful about myself, to be completely frank. Like, I wake up every single morning and I tell myself, "Okay, today is the day. Today I’m going to sit at my desk, I’m going to open my laptop, and I’m going to just do the things I need to do." And I really, truly believe it when I wake up! I have all this motivation. But then... I don't know, by 2 PM I’m sitting on my bed and I realize I spent three hours deep-cleaning my closet or researching something completely random instead of applying for jobs, and I just feel this crushing sense of... I don't even know what to call it. Guilt? Shame? 

It’s just so heavy. And it really, really messes with my mood because I look at my friends from college, and they’re all moving to new cities and starting these shiny new corporate jobs and setting up their 401ks—which I don't even understand how to do, by the way—and I’m just here, stuck, crying in my room because I forgot to pay my phone bill again and my service got suspended. It makes me feel so stupid. I know I'm not stupid, I have a degree, but I feel like a child playing dress-up as an adult. 

So yeah, my well-being is pretty much in the garbage right now. I just feel constantly stressed. It's like this low-level hum of panic all the time, just buzzing in the background, because I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? Like, what did I forget today? Who is mad at me today? Which deadline did I blow right past? It just... it drains all the energy out of me. Sometimes I don't even want to try to make a to-do list anymore because I know I'm just going to lose the piece of paper or ignore the alarm on my phone anyway, and then I'll just end up hating myself even more for failing again.
Do you find it hard to focus on tasks or activities for a long period of time?

Um... I mean, I don't know? Like, what exactly is a long period of time, you know? Because... well, it really depends on what I'm doing. If it's something I'm really, really into—like, I don't know, last week I decided I was going to learn how to knit, and I literally sat there for eight hours straight watching YouTube tutorials and trying to make this scarf. I didn't eat, I didn't drink water, I just sat there. But then... if it's something I don't want to do? Like, updating my resume or reading a contract or even just watching a movie that someone else picked out and I'm not super invested in? I can't do it. I just can't. 

Like, I'll sit down to read an article for research or whatever, and I'll read the first sentence, and then suddenly I'm thinking about how I need to buy more laundry detergent, and then I'm wondering if they still make that one brand my mom used to buy when I was a kid, and then I'm on my phone googling 90s laundry detergent commercials. And then twenty minutes later I realize I haven't read past the first line of the article. So... I guess I'm not sure if it's hard for me to focus for a long time, because sometimes I can focus for way too long, but other times I can't even focus for two minutes. Does that make sense? I don't know if that actually answers your question.
Do you often find yourself being excessively restless or fidgety?

Oh, God, yes. Constantly. It's actually—well, it's really uncomfortable, to be honest. It’s like... okay, so you know when you shake up a soda can and you can just feel all the carbonation pressing against the aluminum, just waiting to explode? That is exactly what my entire body feels like most of the time when I'm forced to just sit there. 

Like, if I have to sit through a job interview—which is already stressful enough, right?—or if I'm on a Zoom call, or even if I'm just trying to watch a movie with my roommates in the living room... I just get this overwhelming, intense pressure building up inside my chest and my arms and my legs. It’s like my muscles are humming or vibrating, and my brain starts screaming at me that I need to move. I need to get up, I need to shift my weight, I need to bounce my leg, I need to play with a pen or pick at my cuticles or twist my rings around. 

If I try to just sit perfectly still like a normal person, I literally feel like I'm going to crawl out of my own skin. It's almost physically painful to not move. I remember in college, my professors would always look at me during lectures because I was constantly shifting in my seat, crossing and uncrossing my legs, tapping my foot, playing with my hair... I just couldn't stop. And even now, if I go to a movie theater, I'm the worst person to sit next to because I can't just sit back and watch the screen. I'm adjusting my posture every five minutes, I'm stretching my arms, I'm shaking my leg. It’s like my body just refuses to power down, even when I'm supposed to be relaxing. It's exhausting, honestly, feeling like you have a motor inside you that you can't ever turn off.
Do you find that your emotions shift rapidly or unexpectedly throughout the day?

Um, rapidly shifting emotions? I don't... I don't really think so? I mean, I don't know what you mean by "unexpectedly." Like, obviously if something bad happens, I get sad, and if something good happens, I get happy, but I don't think I just randomly start crying or getting angry for absolutely no reason, you know? 

Like, I know some people have those days where they wake up and they're just in a terrible mood and they snap at everyone, and then two hours later they're completely fine and laughing, but I don't really feel like I do that. My moods are pretty tied to whatever is going on around me. Like I was saying earlier about feeling so awful about myself when I don't get things done—that's a pretty consistent feeling. It's not like I'm suddenly thrilled about my life an hour after realizing I blew a deadline. I stay pretty upset about it. 

I mean, maybe I get frustrated easily? Like if my computer freezes when I'm in the middle of trying to force myself to write a cover letter, I might want to throw it out the window, but I feel like that's a normal reaction to technology being terrible, right? It's not like a random mood swing. I just... I don't think my emotions are bouncing all over the place without a cause. They're just mostly... heavy, like I said. Just a lot of stress and guilt that kind of hangs around all day. So, no, I wouldn't say they shift rapidly. Does that make sense? I'm not really sure if that's what you were asking.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?

Um, acting on impulse? Like, doing things without thinking? I don't... I don't really think I do that. At least, not in a way that feels like a big problem, I guess? 

I mean, I know some people will just, like, spontaneously book a flight to Europe or, you know, buy a brand new car without checking their bank account or something crazy like that. I definitely don't do things like that. I'm actually a pretty anxious person when it comes to big decisions. Like, when I was trying to decide what to major in, I must have made a hundred different pro and con lists, and I talked to every single advisor, and I still didn't declare until the very last possible second. So I definitely overthink things a lot of the time rather than just jumping in.

And, like, with money... I mean, I'm not working right now, obviously, so I have to be really careful. I might buy, like, a coffee or a new notebook if I see a really pretty one at the store—because I'm always convinced a new notebook will finally be the thing that gets me organized, which is stupid, I know, because I have like twenty empty ones on my desk right now—but that's just small stuff, right? Everyone does that. It's not like I'm blowing my rent money on impulse buys. 

And with people, I don't really blurt things out or do reckless things. I'm usually too worried about what people think of me to just act without thinking. I mean, sometimes I'll interrupt someone when they're talking, but that's just because if I don't say the thought right then, it completely vanishes from my brain forever, not because I'm trying to be impulsive or rude. It's more of a memory thing, I think. 

So, yeah, I don't really feel like I'm an impulsive person. I actually wish I was a little more spontaneous sometimes, because I feel like I get so stuck in my own head about everything. But no, I wouldn't say I act without thinking about the consequences. I usually think about the consequences too much, honestly.
Do you often struggle to initiate tasks or get started on activities, even when you know they need to be done?

Struggle to get started? I mean... I don't know if "struggle" is the right word. I don't think I have a problem starting things, really. Like, I *want* to start them. I know exactly what I need to do. 

For instance, this morning, I knew I needed to start looking for jobs again. I even set my alarm for 8:00 AM, which is early for me since I'm not working, and I made coffee, and I sat down at my desk. I had my laptop open and everything. I was totally ready to start. But then I realized my desk was a little cluttered, and I couldn't possibly focus on job applications with old mail and empty coffee mugs sitting right next to my computer, right? So I decided to just quickly tidy up the desk. 

But then, while I was taking the mugs to the kitchen, I saw that the dishwasher needed to be unloaded, so I started doing that. And then I noticed the sponge smelled weird, so I had to go find a new sponge in the hall closet, but the hall closet was a total disaster, so I ended up pulling everything out of the closet to reorganize it. By the time I finished the closet, it was like 2:00 PM, and I was exhausted, and I still hadn't even looked at a single job posting. 

So it's not that I can't start things. I started organizing the closet just fine! And I started unloading the dishwasher. It's just that I didn't start the *right* thing, I guess? Or I got sidetracked before I could actually begin the thing I sat down to do. But I don't sit there staring at a blank screen, unable to physically begin typing, or anything like that. I just... my path to getting started on the main task is just really, really winding, I suppose. 

And sometimes, yeah, if a task feels really overwhelming—like if it's a huge project with a million steps—I might put it off, but that's just procrastination, right? Everyone procrastinates when they have a big, scary task to do. Like in college, I would always wait until the night before a ten-page paper was due to actually start writing it, but I still got it done eventually. I just needed the pressure of the deadline to kick me into gear. So I wouldn't say I struggle to initiate tasks in general. I just have my own process for getting there, even if it takes me all day and involves cleaning out a closet I didn't even know I was going to clean. Does that make sense? I just don't think it's an inability to start.
Do you find that you can focus on a task for a short period, but then your attention starts to wander?

Um, focus for a short period and then wander? I don't... I don't think that's quite right for me. I don't feel like I have this super short attention span where I can only handle, like, five or ten minutes of something before my brain just checks out. 

Like, if I'm doing something, I can usually just do it. For example, I can sit and watch a really long movie just fine. I watched that new sci-fi movie the other day—well, I say the other day, it was probably last Tuesday, because that's when my roommate had the day off and we ordered takeout—but anyway, it was like two and a half hours long, and I didn't get up once. I didn't even check my phone, which is saying a lot. My roommate was actually getting kind of annoyed because she kept trying to talk to me about what was happening in the plot, and I was just completely glued to the screen and honestly didn't even hear her half the time. So I definitely *can* focus for long periods. It's not like my attention just naturally drifts away after a few minutes like a timer went off.

And even with schoolwork, when I was finishing up my degree last spring, I would go to the library and sit there for literally eight hours straight. I mean, yeah, I might have had fifty different browser tabs open, and I was listening to a true crime podcast while I was typing, and maybe I got up to get snacks from the vending machine a few times, but I was stationed there, you know? I wasn't just wandering off in the middle of a thought or forgetting what I was doing. 

I think it goes back to what I was saying about the closet earlier. Once I actually get into something, I'm pretty much in it until it's done, or until I'm completely exhausted. I didn't just do a tiny bit of organizing and then wander away to go look out the window. I pulled every single thing out of that hall closet and I stayed with it for hours until it was finished. So, no, I wouldn't say my attention wanders after a short period. If anything, I feel like I get really locked in. Does that make sense? I just don't relate to that idea of only being able to focus for a tiny bit at a time.
Do you have trouble calming down after you get upset or angry?

Um, trouble calming down? I mean, no, not really. I actually think I'm the opposite, to be honest. I get over things incredibly fast. Like, almost too fast sometimes? 

I don't really hold onto anger or get stuck in it. If I get upset, it's usually like a quick flash, and then it's just... gone. Like, just the other day—well, maybe it was the weekend, I don't know, time is weird right now since I'm not working—but my roommate, the one I was telling you about with the sci-fi movie? She accidentally threw away this piece of mail I was waiting for. It was just a stupid coupon thing for a furniture store, but I had been planning to use it to buy a new desk chair because my current one is literally falling apart and hurting my back, which probably doesn't help with the whole job application thing I mentioned earlier. Anyway, I was so mad when I realized she tossed it. I was like, ranting in the kitchen, opening the recycling bin, digging through it, just really, really frustrated and venting out loud.

But then, right in the middle of me being upset, my phone buzzed and it was a text from my sister with a picture of her new puppy. And I swear, it was like a switch flipped. I just looked at the puppy, texted her back asking what she named him—it's Buster, by the way, which is kind of generic but cute, I guess—and by the time my roommate walked into the kitchen to apologize and help me look for the coupon, I was already making a sandwich and had completely forgotten I was even mad at her. I literally had to remind myself why my hands were covered in recycling dust. 

So, yeah, I definitely don't stay worked up. If anything, my mom always used to say I was like a summer thunderstorm, you know? Like, a lot of noise for a few minutes and then the sun comes right back out and I'm totally fine and talking about something completely different. I just don't have the energy to stay mad, or maybe my brain just moves on to the next thing too quickly to hold a grudge. So no, I wouldn't say I have trouble calming down at all. I honestly just forget I was even upset in the first place.
Do you experience any physical complaints such as headaches or stomachaches?

Headaches or stomachaches? Um... let me think. Not really? I mean, I don't have any chronic physical stuff going on like that. 

Obviously, I'll get a headache every once in a while, but it's almost always my own fault. Like, I have this giant insulated water bottle that I bought specifically because I kept forgetting to drink water, and I thought having one with a straw would make it easier to just sip on mindlessly? But half the time I just leave it sitting on the kitchen counter, and then I'll be sitting at my desk for six hours straight, just running on the iced coffee I made at like 9 AM. So yeah, by the late afternoon my head might be pounding a little bit, but that's just dehydration, you know? As soon as I realize what I've done and go chug a glass of water, it goes right away. It's not like a real, medical headache. My mom actually used to get terrible migraines when I was growing up—like, she'd have to go shut herself in her bedroom with all the curtains drawn and a cold washcloth over her eyes for the entire day, and my sister and I would have to tiptoe around the house so we wouldn't make any noise. I always felt so awful for her, but thankfully I never inherited that at all. I've never had a migraine in my life.

And as for stomachaches... no, my stomach is usually pretty invincible. I mean, sometimes I'll eat really weird meals because the thought of actually cooking a real dinner feels like way too much effort, so I'll just eat, I don't know, half a box of dry cereal and some string cheese at ten o'clock at night while I'm watching YouTube. So maybe I'll feel a little heavy or gross after that, but it's not a real stomachache. It's just the consequences of my own terrible eating habits, I guess! 

But as far as actual, unexplained physical complaints or just feeling sick for no reason? No, I really don't experience anything like that. I'm generally pretty healthy physically, so I wouldn't say I have any issues there.
Do you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh my gosh, yes. Constantly. That is actually one of my worst habits, and it's been causing me so much trouble lately, especially since I've been doing all these job interviews since I graduated. It's like... I'll be in a conversation, or an interview, and the other person will start asking a question, and my brain just immediately fills in the blank. I think I know exactly where they are going with their thought, so I just jump in before they're even close to being done speaking. 

Like, I had this Zoom interview last week for this entry-level communications role—which, honestly, I'm not even sure I want, but the job market is terrible right now so I'm just applying everywhere—and the hiring manager started asking me about my senior capstone project. And I just immediately cut him off and launched into this whole five-minute explanation about my research methods and the team dynamic, because I was so sure he was asking about how I handle group work. But when I finally stopped to take a breath, he just kind of stared at me and was like, "I was actually going to ask what software you used for the presentation." 

It was so humiliating! I totally realized I had answered the wrong question entirely because I just couldn't wait for him to finish. And I do it in casual conversations, too, not just interviews. I do it with my roommate all the time. She'll be telling me a story about her day, and I'll just blurt out the ending I think she's building up to, and half the time I'm wrong, or I just completely derail her train of thought. It's not that I'm trying to be rude or that I don't care what they're saying! It's just that my brain is already ten steps ahead, and I get so eager to respond that the words just fall out of my mouth before I can stop them, and then I have that awful sinking feeling where I realize I completely cut them off again. So, yeah, that is definitely a huge, huge thing for me.
Do you find it hard to control your emotions when you're under stress?

Control my emotions? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, obviously I get stressed, like right now with the whole job hunt thing since I graduated. It is incredibly stressful, especially when you have to upload your resume to a company's portal and then the portal makes you manually type in every single job you've ever had anyway? Which is honestly just a terrible system and it drives me crazy. But when I'm dealing with all that pressure, I don't really get emotional about it. 

Like, I don't burst into tears or start yelling at people or have meltdowns. I think I just sort of... avoid it? Like, if I'm really stressed about writing a cover letter, I won't get angry or sad, I'll just suddenly decide that right then is the perfect time to reorganize my entire closet by color and season, or I'll fall down a massive YouTube rabbit hole watching four-hour video essays about TV shows I haven't even seen. But emotionally, I'm pretty level during all that. I'm not lashing out or losing control.

My sister is the complete opposite, actually. When she's stressed, she gets so emotional. Like when she was planning her wedding last year, she would literally start sobbing if the caterer didn't email her back right away, and I remember just sitting there on her couch while she cried about the exact shade of the dinner napkins, just totally unable to relate. I just don't react that way at all. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I have a hard time controlling my emotions under stress. I just have a hard time actually doing the things that are stressing me out, if that makes sense.
Do you have a hard time waiting for your turn in lines or when engaging in group activities?

Oh, absolutely. Waiting is honestly like physical torture for me. It doesn't matter what kind of waiting it is, it just makes me intensely, intensely impatient. Like, if I'm just waiting in a normal line at the grocery store or a coffee shop, and the person in front of me is taking too long to find their debit card or asking the cashier a million questions, I can literally feel my skin crawling. I just end up pulling out my phone and checking it over and over again, swiping through my home screens even if I have absolutely zero new notifications, just because standing there doing nothing and waiting is completely unbearable. 

And it is not just physical lines, either. It is waiting in general. Like with this whole job hunt thing, waiting for a recruiter to call me back or email me an update is agonizing. I will sit there staring at my phone, refreshing my email every two minutes, and checking my call log just in case my phone didn't ring and they went straight to voicemail. It makes me so impatient that I just want to push things along, and I have to physically restrain myself from sending them multiple follow-up emails in the same afternoon because I just want an answer right that second. It feels like my entire life is on pause until they get back to me.

And you asked about group activities, which is also a huge yes. I do some group volunteering, sorting donations at a local clothing bank, and sometimes we have to take turns going down the table to log what items we have before we pack the boxes. If the person next to me is hesitating or taking too long to figure out what category a jacket belongs in, I just cannot wait my turn. I will end up interrupting them and just announcing what it is myself, or I will literally reach over and sort it for them just to push things along. I know it probably makes me look super bossy or rude to the other volunteers, but I just cannot stand that feeling of being stuck waiting for someone else to finish what they are doing! It just drives me completely up the wall.
Do you often find yourself feeling unmotivated to do things you know you need to do?

Unmotivated? Um, I don't really think so. I mean, I wouldn't say it's a lack of motivation, exactly. Like, I know I need to do things, and I actually want to do them, but it's more like I just can't get myself to start. So it's not that I don't care or that I'm unmotivated. Like, with the whole job application thing, I really, really want a job. I want to start my career and make money and move out of my current apartment because my roommate is honestly driving me a little crazy with how she leaves her dishes in the sink for days. So the motivation is absolutely there. I'll wake up and think, "Okay, today is the day I'm going to apply to five jobs and revamp my LinkedIn profile." I have the drive to do it. 

But then I sit down at my laptop, and it's like there's this invisible wall between me and the actual task. I'll open a new tab to find a job board, and then I'll remember I need to check my email, and then I'll see a promotional email for a clothing sale, and before I know it, I'm curating an entire cart of clothes I can't afford, and three hours have gone by, and I haven't applied to a single job. But I don't think that means I'm unmotivated! I just get completely derailed. Or I'll look at the application and see that it requires a cover letter, and the thought of having to write one just feels so overwhelmingly exhausting that my brain just sort of shuts down, and I end up doing something else entirely, like deciding I urgently need to deep-clean my baseboards. 

So, I don't think "unmotivated" is the right word for it at all. I have the motivation, I have the desire to get things done, I just... I don't know, I just end up not doing them, or doing literally anything else instead. It's incredibly frustrating because I know how important it is, and I want to do it, but the actual execution just doesn't happen. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel unmotivated. It's more of an execution problem, I guess? If that makes sense.
Do you often make careless mistakes when doing things like job applications or other important tasks?

Oh, careless mistakes... yeah. Yes, definitely. I mean, even with the job applications you just mentioned, I will read over my resume ten times and still somehow submit it with my phone number missing a digit, which is just a whole other nightmare. But it is not just the job hunt stuff. It was actually a really massive issue when I was still doing biotech data work during my degree. 

I was doing this assistant position, and it involved a lot of data entry and running these analysis scripts, and obviously in a lab setting you have to be so incredibly precise. And I would sit there, staring at the screen for hours, and I would be so completely convinced that a script was perfect, or that a massive spreadsheet was completely clean and ready to go. I would feel so good about it. And then, maybe a day later, I would look at it again or someone else would review it, and I would realize I had completely mislabeled a sample ID. Just totally swapped the numbers or typed it wrong. Or I would realize I had just skipped a really important note in the protocol, like my eyes just jumped right over it as if it did not even exist on the page. 

And the documentation was just as bad. I would submit these documentation files, and they would have these glaring, obvious typos. I am talking about words spelled completely wrong, or a sentence that just stops halfway through. And I would look at it later and just be completely baffled, wondering how on earth I did not see that. It is like my brain just autofills what is supposed to be there instead of reading what is actually on the screen. 

And it is so incredibly frustrating because people assume you just do not care, you know? They assume you are just sloppy or rushing and that you didn't check your work. But I did check it. I swear I did. I just literally do not see the mistakes until it is too late. Like with the sample IDs, if you mess one up, it can ruin a whole batch of data analysis, and I would feel so guilty and embarrassed about it. And that is exactly why I get so stressed out about these job portals now, because I just know I am going to miss a typo in a cover letter and the hiring manager is going to toss my application straight in the trash. It just feels like no matter how hard I stare at the page, the mistakes just completely camouflage themselves until the exact second after I hit the submit button. So, yeah, careless mistakes are a huge, huge problem for me.
Do you think your difficulties with organization, time management, and completing tasks are related to problems with focusing attention or something else entirely?

I honestly... I don't really know how to answer that, because I've never really thought about the exact *why* behind it, you know? Like, is it focus? Is it something else entirely? I'm not really sure. I just know it's a complete disaster. 

Like, if you look at my organization skills, or lack thereof, it's just... it's so bad. My bedroom right now looks like a tornado hit it. And it's not like I don't try! I will literally go to Target and buy, like, a hundred dollars worth of those cute acrylic organizers and matching velvet hangers, thinking, "Okay, this is it, this is the system that will finally fix my life and make me an organized person." And I'll spend an entire afternoon meticulously sorting my makeup or color-coordinating my sweaters. But then a week later, there are clothes all over the floor, mail piled up on my desk, half-empty water glasses everywhere... and I don't even know how it happens. Did I lose focus on keeping it clean? Or did I just forget the system existed? I really don't know. 

And time management is the exact same way. It's like time is just this abstract concept that doesn't apply to me, even though I desperately want it to. I will look at the clock and see it's 1:00 PM, and I'll think, "Great, I have plenty of time to get ready for my 2:30 coffee meeting." And then I'll decide to quickly water my plants, which turns into realizing one needs a bigger pot, which turns into repotting a pothos on my kitchen counter, which turns into sweeping the spilled dirt off the floor, which turns into realizing the broom is gross and trying to wash the broom bristles in the sink... and suddenly it's 2:45 and I haven't even put on pants or brushed my teeth. 

So, was I not focusing? I mean, I was incredibly focused on cleaning that broom! Like, intensely focused. But I completely lost track of what I was *supposed* to be doing and the fact that time was actually passing. So I don't know if that means I have a problem with focusing my attention, or if my attention is just completely hijacked by the wrong things, or if it's just some other fundamental flaw in how my brain processes time and priorities. It just feels like a giant tangled mess in my head, and trying to untangle whether it's focus or something else entirely is just... I don't know. I really couldn't tell you the exact root cause of it, I just know it makes trying to function like a normal adult feel completely impossible.
Do you often feel like you are daydreaming or 'spaced out' when you are supposed to be paying attention?

Daydreaming? Um... no. I don't really think so. When I hear "spaced out," I always picture someone just sitting there staring blankly out a window, totally lost in some fantasy world, like thinking about what they would do if they won the lottery or imagining some fake argument in the shower. And that is definitely not me at all. I don't really get that foggy, head-in-the-clouds feeling. 

If I'm supposed to be paying attention to something—like, say, back when I was in my senior year seminars, or even just when my mom calls me to complain about the drama in her neighborhood book club—my brain is never just blank or floating away. It's actually the exact opposite. It's incredibly loud and busy. I'm painfully present, I'm just... not present on the one specific thing I'm *supposed* to be focusing on. 

Like, I'll be looking right at the person who is talking, but instead of hearing their words, I'm noticing the weird, high-pitched humming sound the air conditioner is making, and I'm wondering if the building's maintenance guy ever actually changes the filters. And then that makes me realize I haven't changed the Brita filter in my own fridge in like six months, which reminds me of my roommate and her gross dishes again. So I'm actively thinking about very real, very concrete things. I'm just tuned into fifty different channels at once instead of the one channel I'm supposed to be watching. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I daydream or space out. I never really just zone out into nothingness. I honestly almost wish I did, because spacing out sounds kind of peaceful and relaxing compared to the absolute circus of thoughts going on in my head most of the time! But yeah, no, I don't really relate to the whole daydreaming thing at all.
